title: Mental health
hookLine: saving life includes mental health; asking for help is a mitzvah
tomorrow: a "joke" about Jews lands in the cast chat. what does Noa say?

cards: Two in the morning, a to-do list, and the same words typed to anyone who asks: I'm fine, really. Why is asking for help so hard? Partly because it can feel like failing, as if the strong never need it.
The Talmud tells a story that takes that apart. Rabbi Yochanan was known for lifting people up: when a colleague lay sick, Yochanan visited, said give me your hand, and raised him from his bed.

teach.b: Rabbi Chanina came to see him, said give me your hand, and raised him. The Talmud asks the obvious question: if Yochanan could lift others, why not himself?
The answer is one line: a prisoner can't free himself from prison. Needing a hand isn't a failure of the strong; it's how hands work.

teach.h: LIVE BY THEM, NOT DIE BY THEM.
teach.b: The Torah says of its commandments, "he shall live by them," and the Talmud reads that as live by them, not die by them.
Saving a life, pikuach nefesh, comes before almost every other commandment, and some rabbis today teach plainly that this includes the mind: depression, anxiety, dark thoughts.

teach.h: CARE IN THE HEART: TELL IT.
teach.b: Proverbs says, "Care in the heart of a man boweth it down," and in the Talmud, one rabbi reads the verse as an instruction: tell it to others.
Lived, that looks like telling one person the truth, seeing a doctor or therapist, and checking on the friend who has gone quiet.
If you or someone near you is in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, the suicide and crisis lifeline, or reach local emergency help wherever you are.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, the rabbi who healed others needed someone's hand.

how: Many rabbis and Jewish community groups encourage therapy and talking openly about mental health, citing pikuach nefesh. In danger, in the US call or text 988; elsewhere, call local emergency services.

o: a prayer said only for people in the hospital
caring for the mind as part of guarding a life
keeping your worries private out of modesty

games.q: a hand up — tap the pairs.

s: in the Talmud, the rabbi who healed others could heal himself
Yochanan needed Chanina's hand: a prisoner cannot free himself from prison.
one rabbi in the Talmud reads Proverbs as: tell your worry to others
'care in the heart of a man boweth it down', so speak it out to someone.
asking for help is a sign of weak faith
the Torah guards life, and in the Talmud even great rabbis needed someone to lift them.

games.q: a friend jokes about 'not being around much longer' and quickly changes the subject. what fits today's lesson?
o: ask them kindly and directly, and if they're in danger, call 988 or emergency help with them.
laugh it off with them, so they don't feel awkward about it.
wait to see whether they bring it up again next week.
games.why: saving a life comes first. in the US, 988 is the suicide and crisis lifeline; elsewhere, local emergency help. asking directly doesn't put the idea there.

practice: Rest a hand on your chest and let a few breaths come and go, noticing honestly how you are. Then bring one person to mind, you or someone you love, and version a short message: rough week, can we talk? or how are you, really?
Whether you send it is up to you.

wordCard.voice: Mental health: part of the life the Torah guards. Asking for help, for yourself or someone else, belongs to saving a life.

orig.note: Hebrew: saving a life, which comes before almost every other commandment.

carryVoice: Here's the line: asking for help is holy, and even Rabbi Yochanan needed a hand. Twelve days of community and justice.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 5b (Yochanan raises Chiya bar Abba; Chanina raises Yochanan; 'a prisoner cannot free himself from prison')
Babylonian Talmud Yoma 85b (live by them, not die by them; saving life overrides Shabbat)

sources.q: Care in the heart of a man boweth it down
